meta.level_rule: strong: agreement >= 65%; moderate: at least 10 points above chance and p (corrected for 3 centers) < 0.05; otherwise weak

desouk.q1: How did the heat compare each month?
desouk.a1: Each square compares that month with the same month in other years. The color shows hotter or cooler than usual, and the number is the monthly average in °C.
desouk.n1: Weather = average of the daily high. Satellite = land surface temperature (LST). A grey square means there is no data. Both are compared only from April 2015 to June 2025.
desouk.q2: What does a typical year look like?
desouk.a2: Both sources are coolest in winter and hottest from late spring to summer. The weather high peaks in July (38.1 °C) and the satellite surface temperature peaks in June (35.4 °C).
desouk.n2: Each point is the average of the same calendar month over 10 to 11 years. The two lines measure different things (air high vs ground surface), so compare their shape, not their level.
desouk.q3: Do the weather model and the satellite agree?
desouk.a3: They follow the same yearly shape and agree on hotter or cooler months more often than chance, but not always. Neither is an instrument measuring in your field.
desouk.numbers: They agreed in 59 of 123 months (48%). If each were guessing, they would agree in about 34% of months. That is clearly above guessing, and unlikely to be chance.
desouk.opposite: In 18 months they pointed in opposite directions (one hotter than usual, the other cooler).
desouk.gap: On average the satellite surface temperature is 2.2 °C below the weather high at this center. A gap is expected: surface temperature and air temperature are not the same thing.
desouk.possible_reason: One possible reason for the disagreements is the difference in resolution and in what each product measures. This is a possibility, not proven.
desouk.you_row: You: put a thermometer in the shade in your own field and compare it with this card. Your own reading is the ground measurement we do not have.

ui.subtitle: Interactive preview with real data · Heat Stress layer
ui.daily_title: Daily highest temperature and unusual days
ui.daily_note: Red dots are days unusually hotter than normal for that time of year, blue dots unusually cooler. Click the chart to open that day in the card.
ui.cmp_intro: The weather model is the main source on this page. The satellite is used only as a second opinion.
ui.area_warning: These numbers describe the whole area, not your field.
ui.shared_note: Baltim and Sidi Salem receive exactly the same weather values, because the weather model is coarser than the distance between them.
ui.report_observed: From 2015 to 2025, the daily high in {name} reached {thr} °C or more on {avg} days a year on average. The hottest day was {hot_day} ({hot_val} °C), and the longest hot spell lasted {spell} days.
ui.report_to_verify: Check the temperature in your own field (a thermometer in the shade), and ask an agricultural extension officer which crop stages are sensitive to heat above {thr} °C.
ui.trend_up: The yearly average high rose by about {t} °C per decade, but this is only {n} years, so it is a hint, not a conclusion.
ui.trend_down: The yearly average high fell by about {t} °C per decade, but this is only {n} years, so it is a hint, not a conclusion.
ui.trend_flat: The yearly average high did not change noticeably, and with only {n} years this is only a hint.

sh.footer: This tool helps you see the picture. Your own decisions, your knowledge of your land, and local agricultural expertise come first.
limits: Heat-stress day here means the daily high reached the threshold (35 °C by default; you can change it). It is a simple count and does not include humidity, wind, or which stage your crop is in.

An unusual day is one whose high is more than the chosen number of standard deviations away from the normal for that date. The normal is the average of the same date (plus or minus 7 days) over 11 years.
Only 11 years are available, so the trend per decade is indicative, not a conclusion.
The weather values come from a model (NASA POWER) at about half a degree resolution. They describe a wide area, not a specific field.
Baltim and Sidi Salem receive exactly the same weather values, because the weather model is coarser than the distance between them. Their satellite values do differ.

The weather model says Desouk's daily high averages 4.3 °C more than the coast, while the satellite surface temperature puts Desouk 0.2 °C lower than the coast (about the same). The two sources disagree about how different these places are. One possible reason is that the coastal weather cell includes sea, which keeps highs lower. This is a possibility, not proven.
Satellite LST is the temperature of the ground surface seen from space, not the air temperature. It is monthly, from April 2015 to June 2025, so the comparison covers 123 months only.
Each calendar month has only 10 to 11 values, so the split into hotter / about usual / cooler is approximate.
The agreement test is run per center. After correcting for 3 centers, all three are unlikely to be chance, but Baltim and Sidi Salem share the same weather values, so they are not independent tests.

gl.short: A day when the highest temperature reaches the threshold (35 °C by default).
A measure of how far a value normally moves away from its average. A bigger number means a more unusual day.
A day whose highest temperature is far above or below normal for that time of year.
The average high and low for the same date over the 11 years of data.
Days in a row at or above the threshold.
Land surface temperature: how hot the ground surface is, seen from a satellite. It is not the air temperature.
A measurement taken with an instrument, or by hand, in the field itself.
The share of months the two sources would agree on if each were just guessing.

src.name: NASA POWER (daily weather)
src.used_for: Daily highest, lowest and average temperature, humidity, rain and root-zone wetness
src.product_and_unit: Temperatures in °C; most likely the 2 m air temperature (daily maximum / minimum). Resolution about half a degree. Root-zone wetness is a 0 to 1 index, not a water percentage.

src.name: Satellite land surface temperature (LST)
src.used_for: Second opinion: monthly surface temperature compared with the weather high
src.type: Satellite product (not a direct field measurement)
src.product_and_unit: Column LST_C, in °C. The exact product name and resolution are not stated in the data file and need to be confirmed.
